author: Rob Stumpf
title: Waymo's Latest Safety Numbers Sure Make Human Drivers Look Bad - NewsBreak
text:
By Rob Stumpf ,
1 days ago Waymo Ojai After 271 million driverless miles, Waymo says its cars were involved in 82% fewer injury-causing crashes than humans. Waymo's latest safety numbers shows just how much safer its cars are for other drivers compared to the national average. It reports 82% fewer injury-causing crashes over more than 270 million miles. This works out to avoiding an estimated 841 crashes with injuries, according to Waymo. Robotaxis are a pretty polarizing subject. People are still a bit distrusting of them—after all, changing out the human brain for some silicon isn't an easy concept to grasp. And with some of the more high-profile screw-ups that the public has seen, it's easy to wag a finger when one passes by.
But when it comes to actually getting into an accident, it turns out that Waymo's robotaxis are actually way less likely to cause injury than when us meatbags are actually in the drivers seat, at least according to the company's publicly shared data.
Waymo Lyft Nashville The data comes from Waymo's latest blog post where it reveals that its cars have 82% fewer incidents that result in an injury when compared to a human driver. And before you think that's just a small sample of driving, Waymo says that figure is its cumulative total as of June and represents over 270 million miles of fully autonomous driving.
For serious crashes, that number moves the needle even more in Waymo's favor.
Data shows that Waymo's cars were involved in 95% fewer collisions that caused serious injury of worse, which effectively represents a 20-fold reduction compared to humans. There were 93% fewer pedestrian incidents that resulted in injuries compared to human drivers. For cyclists and motorcyclists, the figures were 86% and 82%, respectively.
Let's put this into perspective a bit more. Waymo's data shows that, on average, there are 1.9 crashes per million miles (known as "Incidents Per Million Miles") in the U.S. However, in the areas where it operates, the frequency of incidents with an injury reported is higher at around 3.77 IPMM. Waymo's operational total is significantly lower at just 0.67 IPMM. In fact, it even managed to maintain that same statistic in San Francisco where the average figure for humans reached 6.64 IPMM.
There are some asterisks, of course. Waymo's numbers only measured the five metropolitan areas where it operated during the study period. Those national numbers represent everywhere—every road, every human screw-up, and any poorly-designed road structure that might even throw the smartest, most sensor-equipped car in for a loop. Still, even a recent independent study by the IIHS backs up Waymo's point: Its driverless robotaxis crash far less frequently than humans.
So, sure, maybe those Waymos on the road can be a bit of a nuisance to the neighborhood . And maybe they're getting a bunch of parking tickets . And they used to honk in the middle of the night while people were trying to sleep. But there is an undeniable uptick in the safety of passengers and vulnerable road users that's pretty hard to overlook.
Based on its total miles driven, Waymo interprets the data as showing that it avoiding 841 injury-causing crashes over the 271 million miles that its cars have driven without anyone behind the wheel. That's a good figure. As the company expands to more markets— including ones with snow —we'll see how the statistics evolve.
